member.name: T:CsvHelper.CsvDynamicRecord
member.summary: A record read without a record type, by GetRecords<dynamic>(): its fields are members named after the header (record.Name), or Field1, Field2 and so on without a header. It is also a read-only dictionary of the values by name, and parses them with .

remarks.para: A record holds the bytes of its fields, not strings: a value becomes a string when it is read, each time it is read, so the fields you never read cost nothing more. The values are strings ( for one of the reader's ); , such as record.Parse<int>("Count"), parses them as the reader's does.

The records of a reader share its schema, so record.Name is bound once to the column's index, and later reads of it, on any record of the same header, go straight to the field. A column takes precedence over a member of this class with the same name: with a column FieldCount, record.FieldCount is its value.

Records keep their bytes in blocks shared with the records read after them (or, for input in a byte array, in the input itself), so keeping one record keeps its block in memory; makes a copy that holds only its own bytes. Records do not change, so they can be used on any thread.

remarks.para: Fields are written into an internal buffer; I/O only happens in (when the buffer is mostly full), and their async counterparts, so async callers never block.

To write records produced on several threads, write them from one thread, or lock around each whole record, from its first field to . To format records on several threads, use or . The options and the record writers do not change, so they can be shared between threads.

member.name: T:CsvHelper.FloatFormatter
member.summary: Shortest round-trip formatting of and to UTF-8 that produces exactly the bytes of value.TryFormat(utf8Destination, out written, default, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture) on .NET 10.

remarks.para: Digits: Junekey Jeon's Dragonbox algorithm ("Dragonbox: A New Floating-Point Binary-to-Decimal Conversion Algorithm", 2020; reference implementation github.com/jk-jeon/dragonbox) for round-to-nearest-even inputs. It yields the shortest decimal that rounds back to the input (the rounding interval includes its end points when the binary significand is even) and, among those, the one closest to the exact binary value, ties to even. That is the digit string the BCL's Grisu3/Dragon4 produce.

Layout: the BCL's "G" rules for the shortest round-trippable string. Writing the digits as 0.d1d2..dn * 10^scale, scientific notation is used when scale > 17 (double) / 9 (float) or scale < -3, with an exponent of at least two digits and an explicit sign ("1E+17", "1E-05", "5E-324"). Otherwise fixed notation: "0.0001", "123.45", "10000000000000000". Zero is "0" / "-0", NaN is "NaN" whatever its sign, the infinities are "Infinity" / "-Infinity".
On failure (destination too small) nothing is written; on success exactly written bytes are written.

member.name: T:CsvHelper.FloatFormatter.PowerOfTwoQuirk
member.summary: .NET 10 runtimes up to at least 10.0.12 have a Dragon4 bug (dotnet/runtime#135582, fixed for a later servicing release by #135614): the "unequal margins" test for exact powers of two is mantissa == (1U << 52), and C# masks that shift to 1U << 20.
